title: Microkernel in Operating Systems - GeeksforGeeks
content:
A microkernel is a minimal operating system kernel that provides only the basic services required to run the system. It uses Inter-Process Communication (IPC) to allow different system components to communicate.

Kernel

A kernel is the core part of an operating system that manages system resources and connects applications with computer hardware. It is one of the first programs loaded during system startup, after the bootloader.

  • Manages system resources such as memory and processes
  • Acts as a bridge between applications and hardware
  • Loads during system startup after the bootloader

MicroKernel

A microkernel is an operating system architecture that follows a minimalist approach. It keeps only essential services in kernel space, while other services run as user-level processes.

  • Essential services include memory management, process scheduling, and IPC.
  • Device drivers, file systems, and network services run in user space.
  • User-level services communicate with the microkernel through message passing.
  • Separating services makes the OS easier to modify and maintain.

Kernel Mode and User Mode of CPU Operation

The CPU mainly works in two modes: Kernel Mode and User Mode. Kernel Mode provides higher privileges for the operating system, while User Mode is used by normal applications.

  • Kernel Mode is used for protected operating system operations.
  • User Mode runs normal applications with limited privileges.
  • This separation prevents user programs from directly accessing or modifying critical OS resources.
  • Normal instructions such as ADD and PUSH can run in User Mode.

Transition from User Mode to Kernel Mode

When a user program needs a service from the operating system, it makes a system call. This causes the CPU to switch from User Mode to Kernel Mode.

  • The system call triggers a software interrupt.
  • The CPU transfers control to the OS.
  • The OS performs the requested operation.
  • After completing the operation, control returns to the user program.

Illegal Operations

  • If a program tries to access restricted memory or execute a privileged instruction, the OS is notified.
  • The OS can display an error, log the issue, or terminate the program.

Virtualization

  • Virtualized systems may provide an additional mode for the Virtual Machine Manager (VMM).
  • The VMM has more privileges than user programs but fewer than the main kernel.

Examples of microkernel-based operating systems include L4, QNX, and MINIX.

Kernel Mode vs User Mode

Used byOperating SystemUser Applications
PrivilegesHigh privilegesLimited privileges
AccessCan access hardware and system resourcesRestricted access to system resources
PurposePerforms protected OS operationsRuns normal application programs
System CallsHandles system callsRequests services through system calls
SecurityMore powerful, so carefully controlledPrevents applications from affecting the OS
ExampleMemory management, device controlText editor, browser, calculator

Microkernel Architecture

A microkernel keeps only the most important services inside the kernel. Other OS services, such as device drivers and file systems, run separately in user space. This makes the operating system more secure, flexible, and easier to maintain.

The main services handled by the microkernel

  • Inter Process-Communication
  • Memory Management
  • CPU-Scheduling

Features of Microkernel-Based Operating System

  • Provides only basic services such as CPU scheduling, memory management, and IPC in the kernel.
  • Runs other services, such as device drivers, in user space.
  • Keeps system services separate and independent.
  • Allows individual components to be updated or replaced easily.
  • A failure in one service is less likely to affect the entire system.
  • Makes debugging, maintenance, and adding new features easier.

Advantages

  • Services are separated, so they can be developed and maintained independently.
  • Only essential functions run in the kernel, improving resource usage.
  • A smaller kernel improves security and reduces the impact of harmful programs.
  • The simpler design improves system reliability and stability.
  • Can be easily adapted to different hardware and system requirements.
  • Easy to port to different hardware platforms, especially for embedded systems.

Disadvantages

  • Message passing between processes can reduce performance.
  • The modular design can make development more complex.
  • Separation between kernel and user-level services can limit performance optimization.
